#!/bin/bash
# Java Application Installation Script
#
# Server Files: /mnt/server

set -euo pipefail

# Install only essential packages for running Java applications
apt update
apt install -y git curl

mkdir -p /mnt/server
cd /mnt/server

# The volume belongs to the node's container user and this script runs as
# root, so git calls it "dubious ownership" and refuses every command
# against it -- including the git init/clone below.
export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1
export GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=safe.directory
export GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=/mnt/server

GIT_ADDRESS="${GIT_ADDRESS:-}"
GIT_BRANCH="${GIT_BRANCH:-}"
GIT_USERNAME="${GIT_USERNAME:-}"
GIT_ACCESS_TOKEN="${GIT_ACCESS_TOKEN:-}"

if [ -n "${GIT_ADDRESS}" ]; then
    ## add git ending if it's not on the address
    if [[ "${GIT_ADDRESS}" != *.git ]]; then
        GIT_ADDRESS="${GIT_ADDRESS}.git"
    fi

    # Git treats a URL as a transport spec, not just an address: schemes like
    # ext:: and fd:: run an arbitrary shell command in place of "fetching a
    # repository", and this variable is a plain user-editable string with
    # nothing else between here and git to stop one. Restricting to http(s)
    # is also what the credential handling below assumes.
    case "${GIT_ADDRESS}" in
        https://* | http://*) ;;
        *)
            echo -e "GIT_ADDRESS must start with http:// or https://, refusing to hand it to git"
            exit 1
            ;;
    esac

    # Credentials go out as a header on the git invocation itself, never folded
    # into the URL. A URL-embedded token is what git would otherwise write
    # verbatim into .git/config, where it sits in plaintext for the life of the
    # server and reappears in `git remote -v` on every future pull.
    AUTH_HEADER=""
    if [ -z "${GIT_USERNAME}" ] && [ -z "${GIT_ACCESS_TOKEN}" ]; then
        echo -e "using anon api call"
    else
        AUTH_HEADER="Authorization: Basic $(printf '%s:%s' "${GIT_USERNAME}" "${GIT_ACCESS_TOKEN}" | base64 -w0)"
    fi

    git_auth() {
        if [ -n "${AUTH_HEADER}" ]; then
            git -c "http.extraHeader=${AUTH_HEADER}" "$@"
        else
            git "$@"
        fi
    }

    ## pull git java repo
    if [ "$(ls -A /mnt/server)" ]; then
        echo -e "/mnt/server directory is not empty."
        ORIGIN=""
        if [ -d .git ]; then
            echo -e ".git directory exists"
            if [ -f .git/config ]; then
                echo -e "loading info from git config"
                # --get exits 1 when the key is absent, which under set -e kills
                # the install right here with no message at all. A .git with no
                # origin is a legitimate state: skip the pull, do not die.
                ORIGIN=$(git config --get remote.origin.url || true)
            else
                echo -e "files found with no git config"
                echo -e "closing out without touching things to not break anything"
                exit 10
            fi
        fi

        # An older version of this script folded the credentials into the remote
        # URL, so a repo cloned back then has "user:token@" in .git/config and will
        # never match the clean address -- the pull would be skipped in silence and
        # the install would still report success. Compare on the address alone, and
        # drop the stored token while we are here.
        ORIGIN_ADDRESS=$(printf '%s' "${ORIGIN}" | sed -E 's#^(https?://)[^/@]*@#\1#')

        if [ "${ORIGIN_ADDRESS}" == "${GIT_ADDRESS}" ]; then
            if [ "${ORIGIN}" != "${GIT_ADDRESS}" ]; then
                echo -e "dropping credentials an older install stored in the remote URL"
                git remote set-url origin "${GIT_ADDRESS}"
            fi
            echo "pulling latest from github"
            git_auth pull
        fi
    else
        echo -e "/mnt/server is empty.\ncloning files into repo"
        if [ -z "${GIT_BRANCH}" ]; then
            echo -e "cloning default branch"
            git_auth clone "${GIT_ADDRESS}" .
        else
            echo -e "cloning ${GIT_BRANCH}"
            git_auth clone --single-branch --branch "${GIT_BRANCH}" "${GIT_ADDRESS}" .
        fi
    fi
fi


# No `java -version` check here: the pelican installer images carry git, curl and
# unzip and nothing else, so it failed the install for a tool this install never
# uses. The JVM lives in the runtime image, where the startup command runs your
# jar.

# Everything above was written by root, and the server runs as the node's
# container user, which cannot write to root-owned files. The volume's own
# directory already carries the right ownership, so copy it downward instead of
# guessing a uid. Wings chowns after an install too, so on a healthy node this
# is a no-op that costs one pass over the tree.
chown -R --reference=/mnt/server /mnt/server

echo -e "install complete"
exit 0
